results.question: Minister, the Westhaven hospital project was originally announced as a way to replace temporary wards and reduce the distance that residents travel for specialist treatment. Since then, the opening has moved twice, the equipment contract has changed, and the local access road has become a separate item in the council's accounts. Residents need commitments that they can compare with what happens on the ground, rather than another general description of the project's benefits. First, on what exact date does the ministry now expect the hospital to admit its first patients? Second, what is the total approved capital budget when construction, medical equipment and the access road are all included? Third, will you publish the complete independent audit, including its procurement annexes, by 30 June 2027?
results.answer:
I understand the frustration of people who have watched a building appear to be almost finished while continuing to receive appointments at facilities several miles away. The difference between a completed shell and a functioning hospital is substantial. Staff have to be recruited, equipment has to be calibrated, and the clinical teams need to test how patients move between departments. None of that excuses the earlier communication failures. It explains why I would rather give a date that the clinical director has agreed than simply repeat the date that appeared on an old construction schedule.

The hospital will admit its first patients on 15 September 2027. That is the date in the operational plan that I approved yesterday. The first services will be outpatient diagnostics and the day-treatment unit. The emergency department is scheduled to move later, after the ambulance service has completed its simulation exercises. I am spelling out the difference because admitting the first patients does not mean that every department will transfer on the same morning. The first-patient date is a firm commitment in the current plan, and the ministry will publish monthly progress updates against the remaining milestones.

On the finances, the construction programme has an approved ceiling of 138 million pounds. The revised medical-equipment contract is 27 million pounds, including installation and the initial training package. Those amounts cover the buildings and clinical equipment. The access road sits in the regional transport programme, and the council is still reviewing the drainage design and the land required for the junction. Its last public estimate was preliminary. I cannot combine that estimate with the hospital contracts and present the result as one approved budget, because the road allocation has not yet received the council's final approval. The hospital's staffing costs and annual operating budget are also separate from those capital figures.

As for the audit, I will not publish the procurement annexes by 30 June. They contain supplier information that is currently subject to a contractual confidentiality process, and I am not authorising their release while that process is unresolved. The audit's general recommendations can be published sooner, and the committee can receive a briefing on the changes we have already made. That briefing is different from releasing the entire document. I recognise that members may consider the distinction unsatisfactory, but I want to be clear about what I am and am not agreeing to release. The procurement team will return with a timetable once the confidentiality review is finished. Meanwhile, we have introduced a register of contract changes and a requirement for the project board to record who approves each variation.

results.question: Minister, the winter electricity rebate has been presented as a targeted response to high household bills, while the associated grid-upgrade programme has been awarded through an accelerated procurement route. Several details remain difficult to reconcile across the household leaflet, the budget statement and the department's announcements. I would like to keep three points separate. First, what is the exact annual gross household-income threshold at which a family stops qualifying for the rebate? Second, did you personally sign the direction that allowed Brightfield Grid to receive the accelerated grid-upgrade contract? Third, how much of the programme's total spending will go to rural households rather than urban households? These questions concern the eligibility rule, your own decision and the geographical distribution of the money, respectively.
results.answer:
The scheme has to be understandable to someone who is looking at an electricity bill at the kitchen table, not only to somebody who spends their working day reading budget documents. That is why the department is replacing the long guidance booklet with a two-page explanation and a telephone service for households whose income changes during the year. We also recognise that gross income does not describe every family's circumstances. Disability-related expenses and the number of adults in a household can affect how far an income stretches, although those considerations are dealt with through separate support schemes rather than this rebate's basic eligibility rule.

For the income rule you have asked about, consider the two adjacent entries in the eligibility table. A household with an annual gross income of 27,999 pounds remains within the eligible group. A household with an annual gross income of 28,000 pounds is outside it. The same comparison applies whether the income comes from one earner or several people in the household. I have described the boundary using those entries because some of the older leaflets used the phrase 'up to' without explaining whether the endpoint was included. We have instructed the helpline to use the table and to avoid that ambiguous wording. Eligibility is assessed using the previous tax year's recorded household income, with a review route for a substantial subsequent change.

Turning to Brightfield Grid, the accelerated route was introduced because replacing vulnerable substations before the winter was important for the reliability of the whole network. Contractors still had to demonstrate that they could meet the engineering standards, maintain a local workforce and provide a workable timetable. But the wider point is that this investment gives communities a chance to build skills that will remain useful after the immediate project has finished. Apprenticeships in electrical maintenance, installation and safety inspection are part of the programme's long-term value. I would like the committee to look closely at how those opportunities reach smaller towns, because people should be able to find skilled work without having to move to the capital. That is the practical outcome on which I want the programme to be judged.

On the rural and urban spending split, I do not know the amount that will go to rural households. I do not have a reliable figure to give the committee today. The application register contains household addresses, but the analytical team has not yet checked the geographical coding against the classification used in the budget tables. I will ask for that breakdown and send it to the committee once it has been verified. Giving a number now would risk confusing the location of a grid investment with the location of the household receiving a rebate. Those are different kinds of expenditure, and the published table needs to distinguish them.

In the meantime, households should continue to apply through the existing service. The department has extended the opening hours of the helpline and has arranged support at local libraries for people who cannot complete an online application. The availability of that assistance does not change the income entries I described. It is intended to prevent eligible households from missing support because they find the application process difficult.

results.question: Minister, after the autumn flooding, the government announced a first phase of neighbourhood protection works and said that the programme would be subject to public scrutiny. The council has since circulated several different maps, while residents have asked for a clearer record of ministerial involvement and maintenance decisions. I have three specific questions. First, which exactly three neighbourhoods are included in the first construction phase, as distinct from areas that are merely being considered for later work? Second, did you visit the Eastbank flood barrier on 12 October 2027? Third, will you publish the barrier's maintenance logs before the committee hearing on 20 November 2027? A list of possible future projects would not identify the first three neighbourhoods, and a description of the department's work would not establish whether you made that particular visit.
results.answer:
I want to begin by recognising the residents who spent those nights moving furniture upstairs, checking on neighbours and trying to keep small businesses open. A flood programme is often described through drawings and engineering specifications, but people experience it through the disruption to ordinary routines. They need to know when a road will close, whether a delivery can reach their shop and how an elderly relative will get to an appointment. The programme office has therefore been asked to work with neighbourhood groups on practical arrangements as well as the design of the barriers themselves.

There are a number of places where the programme can make a real difference: Eastbank, Mill Quarter, South Wharf, Riverside Gardens and the northern part of Old Market all feature prominently in the work we have been discussing with the council. Each has different drainage conditions and a different relationship to the main river channel. Some need changes to pumping capacity, while others need improvements to the way surface water reaches the existing channels. I would encourage residents in all of those areas to attend the programme office's information sessions. The engineers will explain the local proposals and gather information about access problems that may not appear on the central maps. We should use that local knowledge rather than assume that one standard design will work everywhere.

I also want to say something about the government's overseas trade programme. Manufacturers in our region have recently secured new distribution agreements, and the export service is helping smaller firms navigate customs paperwork. That work matters for employment, particularly for businesses that cannot afford a permanent team of advisers. We are expanding the service's appointments outside the capital and introducing a shared booking system so that companies do not have to repeat the same information to several departments. The response from regional business associations has been encouraging, and I expect to report further progress to Parliament later this year.

On your question about publishing maintenance logs, could you clarify which records you mean? Are you asking for the routine maintenance summaries already supplied to the council, the technicians' complete daily entries, or the underlying inspection photographs and incident records? Those are different sets of documents. I also need to understand whether your request includes entries containing residents' contact details and access arrangements for private properties. I need that clarification before I can answer the publication request or give a commitment against the hearing date. The committee clerk can specify the document set, and the department can then respond to that precise request.

For people currently affected by the works, the local contact line will remain available throughout construction. The programme office has arranged evening sessions for residents who work during the day and will provide printed information for people who prefer it to the online maps. That practical support should continue while the council and the engineers resolve the remaining design details.
